title: Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion
summary: Three close cousins of reading comprehension, asked in banking mains and management exams: pick the best summary of a paragraph, spot the sentence that breaks a theme, or choose the line that completes it. All three reward the same habit — tracking the paragraph's main idea and scope instead of its vocabulary.

subtopics.title: Paragraph summary (main-idea questions)
subtopics.concept: A summary question gives you a short paragraph and four candidate summaries. The right answer states the **main idea** in the **same scope** as the paragraph — nothing more, nothing less. Three things break a summary: it is **too narrow** (only one detail), **too broad** (claims more than the paragraph covers), or **distorted** (adds a judgement the author never made).

tricks.title: Find the topic sentence first
tricks.body: Most exam paragraphs put the main idea in the first or last sentence. Mark it before reading the options — the correct summary will be a tighter version of that sentence.

example.q: "Battery prices have fallen 90% in a decade, so electric two-wheelers now cost less than petrol scooters to run. Sales followed." — the topic sentence is the first one: falling prices drove sales.
example.solution: A summary built on the first sentence (prices fell, sales rose) is correct. Any summary only about "battery chemistry" or "the environment" is off-scope.

tricks.title: The every-word test
tricks.body: Read the option and ask: does the paragraph support **every claim** in this sentence? One unsupported word ("always", "only", "the government must") disqualifies it.

example.q: Option: "Remote work will replace offices everywhere." Paragraph says some firms cut space.
example.solution: "Everywhere" and "will replace" go beyond the paragraph — a distortion. Reject.

tricks.title: Cut the extremes
tricks.body: Options with strongest words — *always, never, only, must, prove* — are usually wrong summaries. Real authors hedge; good summaries hedge too.

example.q: Two options look close; one says "can reduce" and the other "will eliminate".
example.solution: Choose the hedged one ("can reduce") unless the paragraph itself claims total elimination.

mistakes: Picking the summary of one example or statistic from the middle of the paragraph — that is a detail, not the main idea.
Choosing an option because it uses the same words as the paragraph; wrong options often copy words but swap the claim.
Letting your own opinion fill the gap — the summary must contain only what the author said.
subtopics.notes:
### What a summary must do
A good summary is a compressed copy of the paragraph's **main idea**. It keeps the author's **scope** (how much the claim covers) and **tone** (how strongly it is claimed). It does not add reasons, examples, or advice the paragraph never gave.

When you compare two options that both look true, do not ask *which is true?* — ask *which one covers the whole paragraph and only the paragraph?* A true sentence can still be a wrong summary if it covers only part of the idea.

### The three standard wrong options
1. **Too narrow** — summarizes one supporting detail. Signal: names one example, one city, one number from the middle of the paragraph.
2. **Too broad** — stretches the claim to a bigger topic. Signal: bigger words like *society, the economy, always, the future of…*.
3. **Distorted** — keeps the topic but changes the claim: swaps a possibility for a certainty, a description for a recommendation, or a small cause for the main cause.

### A 3-step method
1. Read the paragraph and say the main idea in your own 5–7 words **before** looking at the options.
2. Reject every option that adds, removes, or strengthens a claim.
3. Between the survivors, choose the one whose **scope matches**: if the paragraph discussed one city, the summary must not claim a national trend; if it gave two sides, the summary must not pick a side.

### Scope check with an example
Paragraph: *In Bengaluru, carpooling apps cut rush-hour trip times by a fifth last winter. The civic body now wants dedicated carpool lanes.*
- "Carpooling reduced congestion in one Indian city" — right scope (one city, one effect).
- "Carpooling is the answer to urban pollution" — too broad (pollution never came up).
- "Carpool lanes will cut travel times by 20%" — distortion (the lanes are a *plan*, the 20% was measured for the apps).
- "Bengaluru has the worst traffic in India" — new claim, not in the paragraph.

### Quick revision
- Main idea + same scope + same tone = summary.
- Kill narrow, broad, and distorted options first.
- Do the every-word test on the final two options.
- Hedge words in the option usually match a hedged author; absolutes usually do not.

### Worked micro-example
Paragraph: *The state's new fire-safety audit found 60% of city malls with blocked rear exits; three chains fixed them within a week, the rest sought time.*
- Own-words main idea: **audits exposed blocked exits; some acted fast, most stalled.**
- Option "Fire safety in malls needs attention" — too vague, loses both halves.
- Option "Three chains are the most responsible mall owners" — distorts (they are a minority that complied).
- Option "Most malls delayed fixing blocked exits found by the new audit" — right scope and both halves. ✓

patterns.name: Best summary of the paragraph
patterns.howToSpot: "Which of the following best expresses the main idea / central thought?"
steps: State the main idea in 5–7 of your own words.
Reject options that add or strengthen claims.
Between survivors, match the scope.
patterns.why: The correct summary must compress the whole paragraph, and only the paragraph.

example.q:
Urban farms cut food miles and give city groups a shared hobby. But most fail within three years because land rent eats the profits.
Which option best captures the paragraph?
example.solution: Correct: "Urban farms offer real benefits but rarely survive financially." Narrow options quote only the hobby or only the rent; a broad one would claim farming's future is urban.

patterns.name: Author's argument in one line
patterns.howToSpot: The paragraph argues a position (should/must/because), and the options are one-line versions of positions.
steps: Find what the author wants changed or defended.
Keep the author's strength of claim.
Reject stronger or weaker versions.
patterns.why: Argument paragraphs hinge on the author's stance, not on the facts quoted.

example.q: "Public libraries must open earlier, because job-seekers need computers before office hours." Author's stance?
example.solution: Correct keeps *must* + the reason (early hours for job-seekers). An option saying libraries "could consider" weakens the claim; one demanding free Wi-Fi adds a new demand.

patterns.name: Which option is NOT supported
patterns.howToSpot: "Which of the following is not supported by / cannot be inferred from the passage?"
steps: Test each option against the text, sentence by sentence.
Three will have direct textual anchors.
The unsupported one usually stretches scope or adds a cause.
patterns.why: Three options are paraphrases of the text; only one silently adds new information.

example.q: Paragraph: rooftop solar grew fastest in Gujarat last year. Option: "Gujarat leads India in rooftop solar adoption."
example.solution: "Grew fastest" supports "leads in growth", not necessarily "leads in total adoption" — that subtle swap is the unsupported option.

patterns.name: Best title
patterns.howToSpot: "Choose the most appropriate title for the passage."
steps: Capture the topic + the angle in 6–10 words.
Reject titles that are only about one example.
Reject titles that promise a bigger story than the text delivers.
patterns.why: A title is a summary in noun form — the same scope rules apply.

example.q: Paragraph on how Delhi's bus depots switched to electric and drivers retrained.
example.solution: "Delhi's electric bus shift — and its drivers" beats "The future of transport" (too broad) and "One depot's story" (too narrow).

revision: Summary = main idea + same scope + same tone.
Wrong options are narrow, broad, or distorted.
Do the every-word test on the last two options.

subtopics.title: Odd sentence out
subtopics.concept: You get four or five sentences that mostly build one theme, and one sentence that does not belong. The odd sentence usually shares some **words** with the theme — that is the trap. Test what the sentences **do**, not what they mention: the theme is an idea (a cause, a process, a place, an event), and four sentences push that idea forward while one quietly serves a different idea.

tricks.title: Name the theme in 3 words
tricks.body: After reading all sentences, say the theme in three words (e.g. "mangroves protect coasts"). Any sentence that is not doing exactly that job is the odd one.

example.q: Four sentences on mangroves blocking cyclone waves; one sentence names a cyclone's wind speed.
example.solution: The wind-speed sentence mentions the same cyclone but is about meteorology, not protection — odd one out.

tricks.title: Watch the scope shift
tricks.body: The intruder often stays on-topic but shifts level: the paragraph is about a national programme and the odd sentence talks about one person's profit, or vice versa.

example.q: Four sentences on a vaccination drive's logistics; one says "Vaccine makers posted record profits."
example.solution: Same subject family, different scope (business results vs. drive logistics) — odd one.

tricks.title: Check time and place anchors
tricks.body: If four sentences live in one time period or one place and one floats to another era or region for no reason, that one is out.

example.q: Four sentences on this year's monsoon onset; one describes a 19th-century famine.
example.solution: The historical sentence is off the time anchor — odd one.

mistakes: Picking the sentence with the rarest word instead of the sentence that breaks the theme's job.
Keeping a sentence that merely mentions the theme's topic but actually develops a different point.
Choosing an odd sentence that is simply harder to understand — difficulty is not the test; relevance is.
subtopics.notes:
### The theme is a job, not a topic
Four sentences work together like a small team: each one advances the same job. The odd sentence is the one doing a **different job** while wearing similar clothes. So after your first read, complete this line: *"All the sentences except one are about…"* — and finish it with a verb-ish idea (protecting coasts, cutting costs, explaining a rule), not just a noun (cyclones, money, law).

### Four common intruder types
1. **Topic-mate, different job** — talks about the same subject (e.g. the same sport, the same chemical) but serves another purpose: a profit line inside a logistics paragraph.
2. **Scope shift** — national ↔ local, general rule ↔ one celebrity example, cause ↔ business result.
3. **Time or place shift** — the paragraph sits in one period/region; the intruder floats elsewhere with no bridging words.
4. **Direction shift** — four sentences build one chain (problem → cause → fix); the intruder starts a different chain that goes nowhere.

### A reliable method
1. Read all five sentences once for the flavour, then name the theme's job in 3 words.
2. Underline the subject + verb of each sentence (what is each one *doing*?).
3. The sentence whose *doing* does not serve the named job is your answer — even if it shares the most vocabulary with the others.
4. Final check: remove the suspect and see whether the rest flow as one clean paragraph. If the remaining four still feel broken, you removed the wrong one.

### Quick revision
- Name the theme as a job (verb idea), not a topic (noun).
- Shared vocabulary is the trap; shared *purpose* is the test.
- Intruders shift scope, time, place, or direction.
- Removing the right sentence leaves a smooth paragraph.

### A full walk-through
Sentences: *(A) Cement demand tracks infrastructure spending closely. (B) Housing starts lifted cement sales last quarter. (C) The festival season usually sees a paint sales spike. (D) Government road projects added bulk orders for cement makers. (E) Cement prices firmed up in the southern plants.*
- Theme's job: **what is driving cement demand and prices** — A, B, D, E all serve it.
- C talks about **paint**, a neighbouring building-material — the topic-mate trap. Shared folder (home improvement), different job. C is the odd sentence.

### Exam-room method (60–90 seconds)
1. Read the five sentences once at speed — do not solve yet.
2. Write the theme's job in three words in your head.
3. Mentally strike the sentence whose subject+verb does not serve that job.
4. Check the survivor test: the remaining four must read as one paragraph with no gap.
If two candidates feel odd, prefer the one whose *removal* heals the paragraph — relevance always beats rarity.

patterns.name: Topic-mate intruder
patterns.howToSpot: All sentences mention the same broad subject, but one serves a clearly different purpose.
steps: Name the theme's job.
Mark each sentence's purpose.
Pick the sentence serving a different purpose.
patterns.why: Exam writers reuse the topic words across all five sentences to defeat keyword spotting.

example.q: A–D describe how UPI made small-shop payments instant; E says "Smartphone prices fell sharply last year."
example.solution: E touches the same digital ecosystem but is about hardware prices, not payment behaviour — odd one.

patterns.name: Scope shift
patterns.howToSpot: Four sentences stay at one level (national programme); one drops to a personal anecdote or rises to a global claim.
steps: Fix the paragraph's level.
Flag the sentence at a different level.
patterns.why: Level breaks are subtler than topic breaks and test careful reading.

example.q: A–D on India's national rooftop-solar subsidy rules; E on one homeowner's electricity bill.
example.solution: E is a single-household story inside a policy paragraph — odd one.

patterns.name: Time or place shift
patterns.howToSpot: One sentence sits in another era or region with no connector to the rest.
steps: Note the time/place anchor of the majority.
Pick the floating sentence.
patterns.why: Anchors are easy for writers to control and easy for readers to miss under time pressure.

example.q: A–D on this winter's fog delays in north India; E on the 1905 famine.
example.solution: E's anchor is a different century — odd one.

patterns.name: Direction shift (broken chain)
patterns.howToSpot: Four sentences form a problem → cause → fix chain; one starts a chain that goes nowhere.
steps: Trace the chain.
Find the sentence nothing follows from.
patterns.why: Coherence questions test whether you track an argument's flow, not its vocabulary.

example.q: A: A lake filled with weeds. B: Sewage fed the weeds. C: The city diverted the sewage. D: The weeds died back within a year. E: Weeds make good compost.
example.solution: A–D form one story; E is a true fact that interrupts the chain — odd one.

revision: Theme = a job (verb idea), not a topic (noun).
Shared vocabulary is the trap; shared purpose is the test.
Intruders shift scope, time, place, or direction.
Remove the suspect — the rest must read as one clean paragraph.

subtopics.title: Paragraph completion
subtopics.concept: A paragraph stops one step short of its natural end, and you must choose the sentence that completes it. The right closer does two things: it **continues the last thought** (no jump), and it **finishes the paragraph's job** (if the paragraph set up a problem, the closer points at the resolution; if it gave facts, the closer draws the takeaway). Wrong options start a new idea, repeat an earlier sentence, or contradict the direction.

tricks.title: Predict before you peek
tricks.body: Cover the options and finish the paragraph in your own words. Then pick the option closest to your prediction.

example.q: "A third of the city's water never reaches a tap because of leaking pipes…" — you should predict something about fixing leaks.
example.solution: An option about new dams or pricing drifts away; the leak-repair option completes the thought.

tricks.title: Match the direction of the last sentence
tricks.body: If the last sentence turns negative (a problem), the closer usually completes that problem or its fix — it should not suddenly turn cheerful unless a contrast word appears.

example.q: "…but charging stations remain rare outside metros."
example.solution: A closer like "Until charging spreads, the subsidy helps only some buyers" keeps direction; "EV sales are booming" ignores the turn.

tricks.title: No new characters or claims
tricks.body: The closer may reuse the paragraph's ideas but must not introduce a fresh actor, statistic, or recommendation out of nowhere.

example.q: A paragraph about bus routes; an option mentions metro fares.
example.solution: The metro is a new actor — reject.

mistakes: Choosing a sentence that is true and pleasant but belongs to a different paragraph.
Picking an option that merely restates the first sentence instead of moving the thought to its end.
Ignoring the last sentence's direction (contrast or problem) and closing with an unrelated positive note.
subtopics.notes:
### What the last sentence owes you
Every well-built paragraph is a small journey: it opens a point, develops it, and lands somewhere. A completion question hides the landing. So before reading the options, ask: *what is this paragraph building towards?* If it described a problem, the landing is the cost or the fix. If it listed gains, the landing is the catch or the next step. If it argued a case, the landing restates the case with weight.

### Three legal moves for the closer
1. **Draw the takeaway** — compress the paragraph's point into a final judgement ("Fixing leaks must top the summer plan.").
2. **Complete the cause–effect** — finish the chain the last sentence started ("Unless straw finds a market, the smoke returns each November.").
3. **Land the contrast** — if the paragraph turned with *but/yet/however*, the closer resolves that turn, not the opening.

### Three illegal moves (the wrong options)
- **New actor**: introduces a person, scheme, or number the paragraph never mentioned.
- **Echo**: repeats the opening sentence with new decorations — it moves the thought backwards.
- **Overreach**: jumps far beyond the paragraph's scope (from one city's trial to a national revolution).

### Working example
Paragraph: *The city rationalised bus routes after a study showed most buses ran on lines people no longer used. Frequency on the busy corridors doubled.* → The natural landing connects routes-with-demand to better service. A closer like *"Buses that follow demand, not habit, put more service where more people wait"* completes it; an option about metro fares or driver salaries opens a new thread.

### Quick revision
- Predict the landing in your own words before looking at options.
- The closer continues the LAST sentence's direction.
- No new actors, numbers, or schemes in the closer.
- Echo options (rephrasing sentence 1) are traps.

### How wrong options are crafted
Examiners build distractors from the paragraph's own words. Three recipes to watch for:
1. **The echo** — your predicted closer, rearranged to only restate the opening sentence. It feels right and moves nothing.
2. **The true-but-elsewhere** — a factually correct line about the broad topic that belongs to a different paragraph (cheap internet plans in a paragraph about charging stations).
3. **The extra turn** — a closer that adds a *new* contrast or a second conclusion after the paragraph had already landed; if the paragraph made its point, the cleaner ending is the one that stops.

patterns.name: Takeaway closer
patterns.howToSpot: The paragraph gives facts or examples and stops; the options are possible lessons.
steps: Say the paragraph's point in one line.
Pick the option that is exactly that line.
patterns.why: Most completion questions simply test whether you can see the paragraph's own conclusion.

example.q: "Rooftop solar cut the school's bill by 40%, but batteries for night use wiped out the savings." → closer?
example.solution: "Storage, not panels, is where the money question sits" completes the point; an option praising solar ignores the turn.

patterns.name: Cause–effect finisher
patterns.howToSpot: The last sentence sets a cause or condition ("unless…", "if prices rise…").
steps: Trace the chain's next link.
Reject options that jump the chain.
patterns.why: Chain questions test whether you track conditional logic in prose.

example.q: "Punjab's straw has few buyers, so fields keep burning each November." → closer?
example.solution: "A working straw market, not a ban, is what ends the smoke" completes the cause; a stricter-penalty option adds a new remedy the paragraph never set up.

patterns.name: Contrast resolution
patterns.howToSpot: The paragraph turns with but / however near the end.
steps: Identify the two sides of the turn.
Pick the closer that resolves the SECOND side.
patterns.why: After a turn, the paragraph owes the reader a landing on the new side.

example.q: "EV sales doubled on subsidies, yet charging points remain rare outside metros." → closer?
example.solution: "Until charging spreads, the subsidy will keep helping only some buyers" resolves the *yet*; a sales-are-booming option ignores it.

patterns.name: Continuation into detail
patterns.howToSpot: The paragraph is mid-thought and the blank is a natural next detail (still specific to the topic).
steps: Ask what detail the thought demands next.
Reject generalities and new topics.
patterns.why: Some paragraphs end on development, not conclusion — the closer is the next concrete beat.

example.q: "The temple's stone carvings survived eight centuries. The ASI team's first task was drainage…" → closer?
example.solution: "Water, not weather, had been eating the foundations" continues the drainage detail; a heritage-tourism option drifts.

revision: Predict the landing before reading options.
Closer continues the last sentence's direction.
Legal moves: takeaway, chain-finisher, contrast resolution.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A short paragraph followed by four one-line summaries; the stem asks for the main idea or central thought.
pyqPatterns.approach:
State the main idea in your own words first.
Kill narrow, broad and distorted options.

example.q: Paragraph: bus routes redrawn by demand, frequency doubled on busy corridors. Which option best captures it?
example.solution: 'Buses that follow demand put more service where people wait' — the takeaway. Options about fares or metro lines are out of scope.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Five sentences, mostly one theme; the stem asks which one does not belong.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Name the theme as a job in 3 words.
Flag the sentence doing a different job despite shared words.

example.q: Four sentences on UPI's growth at street shops; one on smartphone prices falling.
example.solution: The price line serves hardware, not payments — odd one out, though it shares the digital theme.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A paragraph stops short and four candidate closers are offered.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Predict the landing in your own words.
Pick the closer that continues the last sentence's direction.

example.q: Para on EV subsidy success that turns with 'Yet charging points remain rare outside metros.'
example.solution: 'Until charging spreads, the subsidy helps only some buyers' resolves the turn.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem asks for the most appropriate title.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Topic + angle in 6–10 words.
Reject titles covering only one example or promising a bigger story.

example.q: Paragraph on Delhi's bus depots going electric and drivers retraining.
example.solution: 'Delhi's electric bus shift — and its drivers' beats the broad 'Future of transport'.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: In odd-sentence sets where every option mentions the theme's subject but one changes level (national programme vs one person's story).
pyqPatterns.approach:
Fix the paragraph's level (policy, business, personal).
Pick the sentence at a different level.

example.q: Four lines on a vaccination drive's logistics; one on vaccine makers' record profits.
example.solution: The profit line is business scope inside a logistics paragraph — odd one.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The paragraph's last sentence turns with but / however / yet.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Resolve the second side of the turn, not the first.
Reject options that ignore the turn.

example.q: '…sales doubled on subsidies, yet charging points remain rare outside metros.'
example.solution: The closer must land on the charging gap, not on more sales.

solvedExamples.q:
Choose the best summary.

Chennai's rule that new buildings must install rainwater harvesting looked like paperwork until the last two droughts. Wells in compliant neighbourhoods held water weeks longer, though many older systems now sit silted and unopened.
options: Chennai's groundwater is inexhaustible.
Rainwater harvesting works where it is installed and maintained.
Building rules are always ignored.
Droughts are caused by poor harvesting.
solvedExamples.solution: Main idea: the rule delivered real gains (wells held water longer) with one caveat (unmaintained systems). Option 2 keeps both halves at the same scope; option 1 overstates, option 3 generalises from one case, option 4 distorts causality.
solvedExamples.difficulty: Rule of thumb: a summary must survive every sentence of the paragraph — gains AND caveats.

solvedExamples.q:
Four of the five sentences form one theme. Pick the odd one.

**A.** Corbett's grasslands now hold the country's densest tiger population. **B.** Camera traps photograph new cubs every season. **C.** Relocated villages have allowed prey numbers to recover. **D.** The Brahmaputra floods Assam's fields every monsoon. **E.** Forest guards patrol the corridor at dusk when tigers move.
options: A
B
C
D
solvedExamples.solution: The theme's job is tiger conservation (population, monitoring, habitat recovery, patrolling). D is river flooding — a different job in a different region, though it sits in the same 'nature in India' folder.
solvedExamples.difficulty: Name the theme as a verb-idea, then test each sentence against it.

solvedExamples.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

Every November, Punjab's skies grey out as farmers burn leftover paddy straw; the practice is banned, the fines are on paper, and the smoke returns all the same.
options: The machines that shred straw are cheap and popular.
Unless straw finds a market, no ban will end the smoke.
Delhi's air quality index touches 'severe' each year.
Rice is a water-intensive crop.
solvedExamples.solution: The paragraph establishes: ban exists → burning persists. The logical gap is the absence of an alternative for the straw, so the closer is option 2. Option 1 actually contradicts (if shredders were popular, burning would fall); options 3–4 are true statements from other paragraphs.
solvedExamples.difficulty: Complete the chain the last sentence started — don't start a new one.

practice.q:
Read the paragraph and choose the option that best expresses its main idea.

Companies that moved fully remote cut office costs sharply, and employees saved hours of commuting each week. But managers report that new joiners learn slower without senior colleagues nearby, and several firms have quietly started mentor-buddy programmes.
options: Remote work has failed because new employees cannot learn.
Remote work saves money and time but slows the training of new staff.
Mentor-buddy programmes are the future of corporate HR.
Office rents are falling across big cities.
practice.solution: The paragraph gives two gains (costs, commute) and one cost (slow training for new joiners), ending on the mentor fix. Option 2 covers all of it at the same scope. Option 1 overstates ("has failed"), option 3 promotes a detail into the main idea, option 4 introduces rent markets.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

UPI transactions doubled last year as corner shops adopted QR codes at a stunning pace. Yet in most villages, cash remains the default for wages and groceries, and banks still see their rural branches handling thick bundles of notes.
options: Digital payments are racing ahead, but cash still rules rural India.
UPI has completely replaced cash across India.
Rural banks are inefficient and must be modernised.
Small shops prefer cash because QR codes are costly.
practice.solution: The paragraph states two facts: urban/small-shop digital boom, rural cash dominance. Option 1 matches both. Option 2 contradicts the text, option 3 adds a judgement the text never makes, option 4 invents a cause ("costly").

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

The city's new electric buses cost far less to run per kilometre than the diesel fleet they are replacing. The catch is invisible until nightfall: the charging depots draw so much power that the local grid needs a costly upgrade before the fleet can grow.
options: Electric buses are cheaper to run but need grid investment to scale.
Diesel buses should be banned immediately.
Electric grids across India are on the verge of collapse.
Electric buses cost more than diesel buses overall.
practice.solution: Savings (per-km) + constraint (grid upgrade) is the whole idea. Options 2 and 3 overreach; option 4 distorts — the text says running cost is lower and only scaling needs investment.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

Ocean clean-up arrays now scoop out tonnes of floating plastic each year. Researchers note, though, that rivers carry the majority of plastic into the sea, so every kilo caught offshore is a kilo that leaked past a thousand upstream mouths.
options: Ocean clean-up machines are a waste of money.
Most ocean plastic enters through rivers, so stopping it at the source matters most.
Plastic should be banned worldwide.
Rivers in India are the dirtiest in the world.
practice.solution: The researchers' point is the source-vs-symmetry argument; option 2 states it. Option 1 adds a judgement, options 3 and 4 go far outside the paragraph.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

Trials that pushed school start times later found teenagers sleeping longer and scoring a little better in morning tests. Screens remain the other half of the problem: most students in the trial put their phones down only after midnight.
options: Schools should ban phones entirely.
Later school starts help teen sleep, but late-night screens blunt the gain.
Teenagers are lazier than previous generations.
Morning tests should be abolished in schools.
practice.solution: The paragraph pairs one gain (later starts) with one limiting factor (screens). Option 2 holds both; the others invent bans and judgements.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

A geographic-indication tag for the region's mangoes did what a decade of subsidies could not: export orders rose, middlemen lost their grip on pricing, and growers finally kept a bigger slice of the final sale price.
options: GI tags help farmers earn more than generic subsidies do.
Mangoes are India's most profitable export.
All middlemen should be removed from farm trade.
Subsidies for farmers are useless.
practice.solution: The paragraph's own comparison is GI tag vs subsidies; option 1 states the outcome at the same scope. Options 3 and 4 generalise into policy claims the text does not make.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

Chennai's rule that new buildings must install rainwater harvesting looked like paperwork until the last two droughts. Wells in compliant neighbourhoods held water weeks longer, though many older systems now sit silted and unopened.
options: Rainwater harvesting works where it is installed and maintained.
Chennai's groundwater is inexhaustible.
Building rules are always ignored.
Droughts are caused by poor harvesting.
practice.solution: Gain (wells held longer) + caveat (silted systems) — option 1 covers both. Option 2 overstates, option 3 generalises, option 4 distorts causality.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

In a two-year trial, primary classes that got one weekly chess period saw small but real gains in maths scores, at a cost of a few thousand rupees per school. The scarce resource was not boards but adults who could teach the game.
options: Chess can lift maths learning cheaply; the constraint is trained teachers.
Chess makes children intelligent.
Schools should replace maths periods with chess.
Maths scores cannot improve without technology.
practice.solution: Effect + cost + bottleneck is the full idea; option 1 captures it. Option 2 overclaims, options 3 and 4 invent policies.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

Gig platforms give young workers flexible hours and instant income slips, but pay no provident fund or health cover; policy circles are now debating portable benefits that follow the worker across apps.
options: Gig work trades security for flexibility, and portable benefits are the proposed fix.
Gig platforms exploit workers and must be shut down.
Provident funds should be abolished for gig workers.
Young workers prefer office jobs.
practice.solution: Flexibility + missing security + the policy debate = option 1. Options 2–4 add strong claims the text avoids.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

The newest camera-trap survey counts more snow leopards than any earlier estimate, thanks to hundreds of motion cameras across four states. The species remains fragile: its range spills across borders, and a season of heavy poaching in one valley can undo a decade of gains.
options: Snow leopards are numerous and no longer at risk.
Better surveys find more snow leopards, but cross-border protection decides their future.
Camera traps are the best conservation tool.
Poaching has ended in the Himalayas.
practice.solution: The pairing (better count, still fragile + cross-border) is option 2. Option 1 contradicts, option 3 narrows to a tool, option 4 invents.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

Vertical farms grow lettuce with a tenth of the water open fields need and no pesticide at all. But their LEDs and chillers gulp electricity, which is why the industry has clustered around leafy greens and left staples like wheat alone.
options: Vertical farming saves water but its power costs keep it to high-value crops.
Vertical farming will replace traditional agriculture.
Open-field farming wastes all its water.
Wheat cannot be grown indoors.
practice.solution: Water saving + energy constraint + crop choice is the complete claim; option 1 states it. Option 2 overreaches, option 3 exaggerates, option 4 states an implication as fact too strongly.

practice.q:
Choose the best summary.

Road-safety data shows two-wheeler riders make up nearly half of traffic deaths. Where helmet laws are actually enforced, fatalities fall sharply; camera-based checks have quietly done more than any new advertisement campaign.
options: Enforced helmet rules and camera checks cut two-wheeler deaths.
Two-wheeler riders are careless by nature.
Advertising campaigns save the most lives.
Cars are the safest mode of transport.
practice.solution: The paragraph's own prescription is enforcement + cameras; option 1 mirrors it. Option 3 reverses the text's comparison; the rest invent.

practice.q:
Four of the five sentences below form one theme. Pick the sentence that does not belong.

**A.** Darjeeling's first-flush leaves fetch record prices at spring auctions. **B.** Assam's tea belt employs over half a million pluckers. **C.** Karnataka's coffee estates flood the market during the same picking season. **D.** Chai stalls from Kerala to Kashmir brew the same CTC dust into the morning cup. **E.** Small tea growers now sell directly to city buyers through cooperatives.
options: A
B
C
D
practice.solution: The theme is tea — its economy and culture. Sentence C is about coffee; it shares the plantation setting (the trap) but serves a different crop.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** The monsoon typically sets over the Kerala coast in the first week of June. **B.** A strengthening low-pressure area over the Bay pulls the rain band north. **C.** Farmers advance paddy sowing to catch the first showers. **D.** Dense fog delayed over forty trains in Delhi last January. **E.** Deficient July rain forces the government to release drought advisories.
options: B
C
D
E
practice.solution: Everything works inside the monsoon season's rhythm; D is a winter event in a different region and season.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** India's solar mission originally targeted 20 GW by 2022. **B.** That target was raised to 100 GW as costs fell. **C.** Rooftop solar lagged utility parks for years. **D.** Coal India posted its highest-ever production last fiscal year. **E.** New tenders now bundle solar with storage.
options: B
C
D
E
practice.solution: The theme is solar power's targets and growth; D is coal production — an energy-adjacent intruder.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** Viswanathan Anand became India's first grandmaster in 1988. **B.** Chess coaching academies now dot every mid-sized town. **C.** India sent its largest-ever chess Olympiad team last cycle. **D.** The cricket World Cup final drew a record television audience. **E.** Young grandmasters clock online games between tournaments.
options: B
C
D
E
practice.solution: The theme is chess in India; D is cricket — both are board-and-ball spectacles, which is the trap.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** Sundarban mangroves absorb the first punch of Bay of Bengal cyclones. **B.** Their tangled roots trap silt and actually raise the land. **C.** Fishermen shelter in creek channels when warnings sound. **D.** The Thar desert's thorn forests need almost no rainfall. **E.** Plantation drives replant mangrove saplings after every storm.
options: A
B
C
E
practice.solution: A, B, C, E all work the mangrove theme; D is a different ecosystem entirely.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** UPI crossed ten billion monthly transactions this year. **B.** Even street vendors stick QR codes beside their cash boxes. **C.** The Sensex crossed the 80,000 mark for the first time in July. **D.** Small merchants say settlement now lands the same evening. **E.** Banks have begun nudging customers from cards to UPI for small spends.
options: B
C
D
E
practice.solution: The theme is UPI's growth and usage; C is stock markets — a finance-adjacent intruder.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** Corbett's grasslands now hold the country's densest tiger population. **B.** Camera traps photograph new cubs every season. **C.** Relocated villages have allowed prey numbers to recover. **D.** The Brahmaputra floods Assam's fields every monsoon. **E.** Forest guards patrol the corridor at dusk when tigers move.
options: A
B
C
E
practice.solution: The theme is tiger conservation; D is about floods — riverine, not wildlife management.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** Neeraj Chopra's 88-metre throw rewrote the national record. **B.** Javelin coaches stress a fast run-up over raw arm strength. **C.** Finnaly-gripped spears fly farther in cool evening air. **D.** The morning session of the hockey qualifiers was rained out. **E.** A Medal at the Worlds made him a household name.
options: A
B
C
E
practice.solution: The theme is javelin/athletics; D switches sport (hockey) while staying inside 'sports events'.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** GST merged seventeen taxes into one national levy. **B.** Small businesses file one monthly return instead of a dozen. **C.** The 28% slab now covers only luxury and sin goods. **D.** The old income-tax slabs of the 1990s rose with pay commissions. **E.** E-way bills track goods moving between states.
options: A
B
C
E
practice.solution: The theme is GST's design; D is income tax — another tax, different regime (scope shift).

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** Himalayan springs that fed villages for generations now run dry by March. **B.** Deforestation on recharge slopes is a major cause. **C.** Spring-shed programmes train villagers to dig recharge pits. **D.** Mumbai recorded its wettest July in a decade. **E.** Some panchayats now meter spring water for fair sharing.
options: A
B
C
E
practice.solution: The theme is Himalayan spring depletion and response; D is an unrelated city's rainfall record.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** Pashmina shawls carry a geographical-indication tag to prove Kashmiri origin. **B.** Kancheepuram weavers sign their silk with the same protection. **C.** Machine-made imitations undercut tagged products during festival sales. **D.** ONDC is expanding e-commerce access to small sellers nationwide. **E.** The tag logo now appears on certified handicraft boxes.
options: A
B
C
E
practice.solution: The theme is GI-tagged crafts; D is e-commerce infrastructure — a policy-platform intruder.

practice.q:
Pick the odd sentence.

**A.** The campaign vaccinated a million people on its first day. **B.** Cold-chain vans kept doses at two to eight degrees through the heat. **C.** Asha workers knocked on doors to bring hesitant families in. **D.** Vaccine makers posted record profits that quarter. **E.** Registration portals staggered slots to avoid crowds.
options: A
B
C
E
practice.solution: The theme is the drive's logistics; D shifts scope to companies' business results — the classic topic-mate trap.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

The transport authority redrew the city's bus routes after a study showed buses running on lines people had stopped using. Frequency on the busy corridors doubled within months.
options: Bus fares were kept unchanged through the exercise.
Buses that follow demand, not habit, put more service where more people wait.
The metro is building three new lines nearby.
Drivers had demanded better shifts for years.
practice.solution: The paragraph's point is demand-based planning paying off; option 2 is exactly that takeaway. Options 1, 3, 4 introduce unrelated details.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

Summer water shortages returned to the old neighbourhoods first. Engineers found that nearly a third of the supply leaked away through ageing pipes before it reached any tap.
options: Desalination plants are expensive to run.
Fixing leaks, not just adding supply, must top the city's summer plan.
Water tankers charge steep rates in May.
The reservoirs were built decades ago.
practice.solution: The paragraph sets up leakage as the revealed problem; option 2 completes it with the implied fix. The others are new topics.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

EV sales doubled this year on generous subsidies, and every major maker launched a new model. Yet charging points remain rare outside the metros.
options: Until charging spreads beyond big cities, the subsidy will keep helping only some buyers.
EV sales are expected to double again next year.
Petrol prices have stayed high all year.
The government deserves credit for the scheme.
practice.solution: The paragraph turns with 'Yet'; the closer must resolve the charging-gap, as option 1 does. Option 2 ignores the turn; options 3–4 drift.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

Every November, Punjab's skies grey out as farmers burn leftover paddy straw; the practice is banned, the fines are on paper, and the smoke returns all the same.
options: The machines that shred straw are cheap and popular.
Unless straw finds a market, no ban will end the smoke.
Delhi's air quality index touches 'severe' each year.
Rice is a water-intensive crop.
practice.solution: The paragraph's logic is: ban exists, burning persists → the missing piece is an alternative, i.e. a market for straw. Option 2 lands exactly there.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

The neighbourhood library was dying: three readers a day, broken fans, a librarian counting the months to retirement. Then a volunteer group moved in with story hours on Saturdays, exam desks all summer, and a chai counter run by a self-help group.
options: Libraries are outdated in the age of the internet.
A library thrives when it becomes the neighbourhood's living room, not just a book store.
The municipal budget for libraries has been cut twice.
The librarian finally applied for a transfer.
practice.solution: The paragraph builds the revival with three community uses; option 2 states the lesson inside it. Option 1 contradicts, the others wander.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

The startup printed a family's 60-square-metre house in ten days: walls layer by layer, plumbing conduits set in the print, total cost a third of conventional construction.
options: If costs keep falling, printed walls could house the next million families.
Cement is a major source of carbon emissions.
The family moved to another city soon after.
Conventional builders are well organised.
practice.solution: The paragraph stacks gains (speed, plumbing, cost); option 1 extends them to scale. The others are unrelated or negative drifts.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

Rural clinics post vacancies for years; young doctors cite absent housing, failing schools for their children, and the loneliness of being the only specialist for forty kilometres.
options: Staying needs housing, schools and a decent salary — not posters about duty.
Doctors earn a lot in cities.
The government should build more medical colleges.
Village health centres lack electricity.
practice.solution: The paragraph lists the reasons doctors leave; option 1 converts the list into the closing argument. Options 2–4 open new threads.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

Film tickets in the multiplexes now cost a family of four more than a full month of a streaming subscription, and the popcorn is extra.
options: When an outing costs a month of home viewing, the sofa wins.
Cinemas should screen more regional films.
OTT platforms raise prices every year too.
Families should watch fewer movies.
practice.solution: The paragraph sets up the price comparison; option 1 lands the implied conclusion. Option 3 argues back instead of completing; the rest drift.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

Coastal catches have fallen for a fifth straight year. Big trawlers blame the weather; marine biologists point to Juvenile fish hauled in before they ever spawn, killed by nets with fine mesh.
options: Regulating the smallest net, not just the biggest boat, may decide the coast's future.
Fish prices have risen in city markets.
Monsoon fishing bans are popular with tourists.
Aquaculture is growing in Andhra Pradesh.
practice.solution: The biologists' point is juvenile over-harvesting; option 1 turns it into the closing remedy. The others introduce new topics.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

Free power has pumped groundwater to the surface for decades, and the water table under the farm belt drops by half a metre every year.
options: Power that is free must be used wisely, or the water table pays the bill.
Solar pumps are cheaper to operate than diesel ones.
The power company's losses are mounting.
Farmers grow paddy because of the free power.
practice.solution: The paragraph's chain is free power → over-pumping → falling water table; option 1 completes it. Option 4 repeats a cause as fact; the rest drift.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

India's discarded phones and chargers pile up faster than any formal recycler can process; the informal sector burns boards to recover a few grams of gold.
options: The cheapest gadget carries the heaviest afterlife unless repair and take-back become normal again.
Gold prices have risen sharply this year.
Phone launches happen twice a year now.
Recycling plants need imported machinery.
practice.solution: The paragraph paints the e-waste aftermath; option 1 closes with the implied structural fix. Options 2–4 are details from other stories.

practice.q:
Choose the sentence that best completes the paragraph.

The city filled three lakes for housing schemes in the last decade; this monsoon, the water had nowhere to go and the newest colonies flooded first.
options: Every lake saved from a landfill is a flood that never happens.
Rainfall has increased in recent years.
Housing demand keeps growing in cities.
The colonies were built cheaply.
practice.solution: The paragraph's chain (lakes gone → flooding) begs for that closing line; option 1 states it as a general truth. The rest drift.
